66-001.r: Rowlatt Act (1919) → Government could imprison people without trial (summary procedures), to curb national and revolutionary activity; from 1917 Sedition Committee of Justice Rowlatt (Chelmsford's time).

66-005.r: Rowlatt Act (1919, Gandhi's 'Black Act') based on Sedition Committee; Gandhi used Home Rule League in Rowlatt Satyagraha (both true); Simon Commission came 1928, so 3 false.

66-006.r: Rowlatt Act passed under Viceroy Lord Chelmsford (1916-1921).

66-008.r: Congress opposed Rowlatt Act (March 1919) → it limited individual liberty: trials without jury, detention without proper trial.

66-009.r: Rowlatt Satyagraha → first all-India struggle though largely urban; Rowlatt Act curbed freedom of expression and press, strengthened police powers → both true.

66-010.r: Gandhi's first all-India venture → Rowlatt Satyagraha (1919); Champaran (1917), Ahmedabad (1918), Kheda (1918) were local, issue-specific.

66-011.r: No-tax campaign (non-payment of Lagaan) against Rowlatt Act ('Black Law') → suggested by Swami Shraddhanand.

66-012.r: Anarchical and Revolutionary Crime Act (1919) = Rowlatt Act, passed on recommendations of committee chaired by Justice Sidney Rowlatt.

66-013.r: Event just before Jallianwala Bagh → Rowlatt Act (March 1919); then nationwide strike (6 April) and massacre by General Dyer (13 April 1919).

66-014.r: Jallianwala Bagh massacre, Amritsar → 13 April 1919, during Rowlatt Satyagraha; crowd was protesting repressive measures and arrest of two Punjab leaders.

66-021.r: Rabindranath Tagore returned his Knighthood in protest against Jallianwala Bagh Massacre (13 April 1919); date given as May 30 (question) / May 31 (explanation), 1919.

66-027.r: Tagore renounced Knighthood (A true) in protest against Jallianwala Bagh Massacre, not to join Non-Cooperation (R false).

66-028.r: Resigned from Viceroy's Executive Council over Jallianwala Bagh Massacre → Sir Shankaran Nair.
66-028.t: Tagore returned his Knighthood; Shankaran Nair resigned from the Executive Council.

66-031.r: Gave up title of 'Sir' over Jallianwala Bagh incident → Rabindranath Tagore.

66-032.r: Order: arrest of Dr. Satyapal and Saifuddin Kitchlu (9 April 1919) → Jallianwala Bagh (13 April 1919) → Amritsar Congress Session (December 1919).

66-033.r: Hunter Committee (Disorders Inquiry Committee under Lord William Hunter; 7 members: 4 British, 3 Indian) → set up after Jallianwala Bagh massacre.

66-034.r: Udham Singh shot Michael O'Dwyer (Punjab Lieutenant-Governor at time of Jallianwala Bagh) at Caxton Hall, London, 13 March 1940.

66-037.r: Congress Inquiry Committee report on Jallianwala Bagh → drafted by Mahatma Gandhi (UPPSC dropped this question in its revised key).

66-038.r: Viceroy at Jallianwala Bagh (1919) → Lord Chelmsford; his tenure: Government of India Act 1919 (provincial dyarchy), Rowlatt Act, start of Non-Cooperation.

66-039.r: Montague called the Jallianwala Bagh massacre (1919, Brigadier General Dyer's firing) a 'Preventive Murder'.

66-040.r: Rowlatt Act (March 1919, Justice Sidney Rowlatt commission) → arrest without reason, search without warrant, prison without trial → anger leading to Jallianwala Bagh.

67-001.r: Khilafat Movement → Ali brothers (Muhammad Ali, Shaukat Ali) with Abul Kalam Azad, Hasrat Mohani, Hakim Ajmal Khan; All India Khilafat Committee at Lucknow.
67-001.t: Haji Shariatullah founded the Faraizi Movement, not Khilafat.

67-003.r: Khilafat aims → rouse anti-British feeling among Indian Muslims; save Ottoman empire and preserve the Khilafat (Sultan of Turkey as Caliph).

67-004.r: President, All India Khilafat Conference (1919) → Mahatma Gandhi; he backed Khilafat to win Muslim support and unite Hindus and Muslims against the British.

67-008.r: Hakim Ajmal Khan renounced title 'Haziq-ul-Mulk' (given by British in 1908) during Khilafat agitation.

67-009.r: M.A. Jinnah warned Gandhi not to encourage fanaticism of Muslim religious leaders; he denounced Gandhi's Khilafat support (per K.M. Munshi).

67-011.r: Result of Khilafat Movement → Hindu-Muslim differences narrowed; Gandhi called it a golden opportunity for unity.

67-012.r: Swami Shraddhanand → speech on Hindu-Muslim unity from pulpit of Jama Masjid, Delhi, 4 April 1919, before 30,000 Muslims.

67-013.r: Congress supported Khilafat → to reinstate the Caliph and win Muslim sympathy (Hindu-Muslim unity).

67-014.r: Did not support Khilafat → Pandit Madan Mohan Malviya, who opposed Gandhi's endorsement of it.

67-015.r: Khilafat Committee at Allahabad (June 1920) asked Gandhi to lead Non-Cooperation; Congress special Calcutta session (September 1920, Lala Lajpat Rai) passed the resolution.

67-016.r: Aitchison: 'we could not play off the Mohammedans against the Hindus' → Khilafat and Non-Cooperation Movement (1919-22), a time of rare Hindu-Muslim unity.

67-017.r: Moplah Rebellion (1921) → offshoot of Khilafat Movement; Moplah peasants rose against Hindu landlords allied with the British.

68-001.r: Non-Cooperation resolution: Gandhi moved it at Calcutta special session (September 1920), opposed by C.R. Das; at Nagpur (December 1920) C.R. Das himself moved it.
68-001.t: C.R. Das opposed it at Calcutta but moved it at Nagpur.

68-002.r: Non-Cooperation Movement launched → 1 August 1920; resolution adopted at Calcutta special session, September 1920 (President Lala Lajpat Rai).

68-004.r: First mass movement led by Gandhi → Non-Cooperation (1920-1922); Champaran (1917) was his first movement but local.

68-005.r: Non-Cooperation on Khilafat question → 1920; Calcutta special session (September 1920, Lala Lajpat Rai) discussed Khilafat, Punjab wrongs and Swaraj.

68-006.r: Causes of Non-Cooperation (1 August 1920 to February 1922) → Rowlatt Act, Punjab atrocities (Jallianwala Bagh), Khilafat; Salt Law was not a cause.

68-007.r: Calcutta special session (September 1920) that passed the Non-Cooperation resolution demanding Swaraj → President Lala Lajpat Rai.

68-008.r: Non-Cooperation launched 1 August 1920 → aim 'Swaraj in a year'; lawyers like Motilal Nehru, Rajendra Prasad, Vallabhbhai Patel gave up practice.

68-012.r: Nagpur Session 1920 → goal: Swaraj by peaceful, legitimate means; Non-Cooperation in stages, civil disobedience and tax refusal only if no Swaraj within a year or repression → both true.

68-013.r: Non-Cooperation (1920 to 1922; 'Swaraj within a year'; boycott programme) → M.A. Jinnah did not support it.

68-014.r: Non-Cooperation in towns: students left government schools, teachers resigned, lawyers quit (true); 'only upper castes and rich joined' and 'Justice Party boycotted council elections' are false.

68-015.r: Non-Cooperation's anti-alcohol drive cut revenue → Government of Bihar and Odisha circulated list of famous drinkers (Alexander, Julius Caesar, Napoleon, Shakespeare).

68-016.r: Non-Cooperation led to → Congress as mass movement, Hindu-Muslim unity, fear of British might removed; not British willingness to grant concessions.

68-017.r: Gandhi surrendered 'Kaiser-i-Hind' medal (given 1915 by Lord Hardinge II) in 1920 during Non-Cooperation Movement.

68-018.r: Gave up legal practice in Non-Cooperation → C.R. Das, Motilal Nehru, Rajendra Prasad, Jawaharlal Nehru, Vithalbhai Patel, Vallabhbhai Patel.

68-019.r: Gandhi was arrested on 10 March 1922 (not 1921), after withdrawing Non-Cooperation over Chauri-Chaura; first major public speech at BHU (true).

68-020.r: Tilak supported Non-Cooperation (doubted council-election boycott) but died on its first day, so could not see its result.

68-021.r: Rahul Sankrityayan (Kedar Nath Pandey; 1893-1963; 'Father of Hindi Travel literature') → active in Chhapra, Bihar during Non-Cooperation, with Nagnarayan.

68-022.r: Chauri-Chaura (Gorakhpur district, U.P.) → 4 February 1922; Non-Cooperation protesters set a police station on fire, killing all occupants.

68-025.r: Chauri-Chaura aftermath: 225 arrested, 170 sentenced to death by Gorakhpur Sessions Judge → legal defence by Madan Mohan Malaviya and Krishna Kant.
